title: Alternative Investment Funds (Category I and II) Distributors
blurb: Private equity, venture, debt and real-estate funds explained for distributors: structure, fees, due diligence, documents, valuation and tax.

units.title: Overview of alternative investments
units.overview: What counts as alternative, how it differs from listed equity and debt, and the main strategies.
focus: Private equity, venture, hedge, real assets.
facts: Alternative investments
Alternative investments are assets other than listed equity, bonds and cash, such as private equity, venture capital, hedge funds, real estate and infrastructure.
An investor puts money in an unlisted growth company through a fund.
Alternative investments are the same as listed shares.
Private equity
Private equity invests in unlisted companies, usually taking significant ownership, with the aim of growing value and exiting later.
A fund buys a stake in a private manufacturer to expand it.
Private equity invests only in listed companies.
Venture capital
Venture capital funds early-stage, high-growth companies, accepting high failure rates for the chance of outsized returns.
A fund backs a start-up with a new technology.
Venture capital funds only mature, stable firms.
Hedge fund strategies
Hedge funds use strategies such as long-short, market-neutral, event-driven and macro, often with leverage and derivatives.
A fund buys undervalued shares and sells overvalued ones short.
Hedge funds can only buy and hold equities.
Illiquidity
Alternatives are typically illiquid, with money locked for years and limited exit options before the end of the fund's life.
An investor cannot withdraw until the fund winds up.
Alternatives offer daily redemption.
Low correlation
Many alternatives show low correlation with listed markets, offering diversification, though valuations are less frequent.
A real-estate fund does not move with the stock market.
Alternatives always move exactly with equities.
Manager skill
Returns from alternatives depend heavily on manager skill, so dispersion between top and bottom managers is wide.
The gap between the best and worst PE fund is large.
All alternative managers deliver similar returns.

units.title: Alternative investment funds in India
units.overview: The Indian AIF market, its categories and the investors it serves.
visuals: Venture capital, SME, social venture, infrastructure, angel funds
Invests in sectors the government wants to encourage
PE, debt funds, fund of funds
May use leverage and trade listed derivatives
facts: Alternative Investment Fund
An AIF is a privately pooled investment vehicle that raises money from investors for investing as per a defined policy, regulated by SEBI.
A trust pools ₹100 crore from wealthy investors for private investments.
An AIF raises money from the general public.
Category I AIF
Category I AIFs invest in start-ups, early-stage ventures, SMEs, social ventures and infrastructure that the government considers socially or economically desirable.
A venture capital fund backing start-ups.
Category I AIFs use high leverage.
Category II AIF
Category II AIFs, such as private equity and debt funds, do not undertake leverage except for day-to-day operational needs and are not given specific incentives.
A private equity fund investing in unlisted companies.
Category II AIFs are hedge funds trading with leverage.
Category III AIF
Category III AIFs, such as hedge funds, employ diverse or complex trading strategies and may use leverage and trade listed derivatives.
A long-short equity fund using derivatives.
Category III AIFs cannot use leverage.
Angel fund
An angel fund is a sub-category of Category I that pools money from angel investors to invest in early-stage start-ups, with smaller minimums.
An angel network invests in seed-stage ventures.
An angel fund invests in listed blue-chips.
Minimum investment
Each investor in an AIF must invest at least ₹1 crore, with a lower limit of ₹25 lakh for angel funds and employees or directors of the AIF's manager.
An investor needs to commit at least ₹1 crore.
The minimum investment is ₹10,000.
Minimum corpus
An AIF scheme must have a corpus of at least ₹20 crore (₹5 crore for an angel fund) before it begins investing.
A fund must raise ₹20 crore to begin.
An AIF can start with any amount.
Number of investors
An AIF scheme cannot have more than 1,000 investors (200 for angel funds) as it raises money through private placement.
A scheme caps its investor count at 1,000.
An AIF can have unlimited investors.
Accredited investor
An accredited investor is one who meets income or net worth criteria and is recognised for certain relaxations in the AIF framework.
A highly wealthy investor is certified with an accreditation agency.
An accredited investor is a retail depositor.

units.title: Concepts in the AIF industry
units.overview: The vocabulary of private funds: commitment, drawdown, J-curve, GP and LP, and fees.
facts: Commitment
A commitment is the total amount an investor agrees to invest in the fund, to be called in instalments over time.
An investor commits ₹5 crore but pays as and when the fund asks.
A commitment is paid in full on day one.
Drawdown
A drawdown or capital call is the manager's notice to investors to pay a portion of their commitment for an investment or expenses.
An investor receives a notice asking for 20% of the commitment.
A drawdown is a distribution of profits.
General partner and limited partner
The GP (manager) runs the fund; LPs (investors) provide the capital and have limited liability and no role in daily decisions.
The manager makes investment decisions while investors supply capital.
LPs manage the fund's day-to-day investments.
J-curve
The J-curve describes how returns in a private fund are negative in early years due to fees and unrealised investments, then rise as investments mature and exit.
A fund shows losses in years 1 to 3 and gains later.
Private funds show high returns from the first year.
Management fee
The management fee is a yearly percentage of commitments or invested capital charged to cover the manager's operating costs, regardless of performance.
A manager charges 2% of commitments every year.
The management fee is paid only on profits.
Carried interest
Carried interest is the manager's share of fund profits, commonly 20%, earned after investors receive their capital and preferred return.
The manager gets 20% of profits above the hurdle.
Carried interest is paid before investors get their capital back.
Hurdle rate
The hurdle rate or preferred return is the minimum return investors must receive before the manager earns carry.
Investors get 10% a year before the manager shares profits.
The hurdle rate is the management fee.
Catch-up
A catch-up lets the manager receive a larger share of distributions after the hurdle until it has received its full carry percentage of total profits.
After the hurdle, the manager gets most of the next distributions until it has 20% of profit.
A catch-up reduces the manager's carry.
Clawback
A clawback requires the manager to return excess carry if, over the fund's life, it received more than its entitled share.
The manager repays carry after later losses wipe out earlier profits.
A clawback lets managers keep any carry paid.
Distribution waterfall
The waterfall sets the order in which distributions are paid: return of capital, preferred return, catch-up and then the carry split.
Proceeds first return investors' capital and then pay the hurdle.
The waterfall pays the manager's carry first.
IRR and MOIC
IRR measures annualised return accounting for timing of flows; MOIC is total value divided by invested capital, ignoring time.
A fund returns 2 times the capital over five years.
MOIC accounts for the timing of cash flows.
DPI, RVPI and TVPI
DPI is distributions divided by paid-in capital, RVPI is residual value divided by paid-in capital, and TVPI is their sum.
A fund has returned half of the capital paid in and holds more.
DPI includes unrealised value.
Vintage year
The vintage year is the year in which a fund first invested; funds are compared with others of the same vintage.
A fund launched in 2018 is compared with other 2018 funds.
Vintage year is the year of exit.

units.title: Regulatory framework: Indian context
units.overview: The SEBI (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012 and what they require of funds, sponsors, managers and distributors.
facts: SEBI AIF Regulations 2012
These regulations govern registration, investment conditions, disclosure and operation of AIFs in India.
The rules under which the fund must register and operate.
AIFs are outside SEBI's regulation.
Registration
An AIF must be registered with SEBI under one of the three categories before it raises funds.
A fund obtains a certificate before collecting commitments.
An AIF can start raising money before registration.
Private placement memorandum
The PPM is the offer document of an AIF, filed with SEBI through a merchant banker, describing strategy, fees, risks and terms.
An investor reads the document before committing to the fund.
The PPM is not required for AIFs.
Sponsor and manager commitment
Sponsor or manager must invest in the fund as 'skin in the game': 2.5% of the corpus or ₹5 crore, whichever is lower, for Category I and II.
The sponsor puts its own money in the fund.
Sponsors need not invest in the AIF.
Tenure of Category I and II
Category I and II AIFs must be closed-ended with a minimum tenure of three years, and extension is allowed with investor consent.
A PE fund has a ten-year life with a possible extension.
A Category II fund can be open-ended.
Concentration limit
Category I and II AIFs may not invest more than 25% of investable funds in one investee company.
A fund limits any single investee to a quarter of its funds.
A Category II AIF may invest all funds in one company.
Leverage limits
Category I and II AIFs cannot borrow except for short-term needs, within strict limits, while Category III may use leverage up to a stated limit.
A Category II fund cannot use borrowing to magnify returns.
Category II AIFs may leverage up to 5 times.
Investments in associates
Investments in associates and the manager's related parties need to be disclosed and approved by investors as per the regulations.
A fund invests in a related company only with proper approval.
Related-party investments need no disclosure.
Custodian
AIFs are required to appoint a custodian to safekeep their securities, as mandated by SEBI.
An independent custodian holds the fund's assets.
AIFs hold securities with no custodian.
Benchmarking and reporting
AIFs must report performance to benchmarking agencies recognised by SEBI, supporting comparability and transparency.
A fund's performance is reported to an independent benchmarking provider.
AIFs never report performance.
Distributor requirements
Distributors of AIFs must hold the NISM XIX-A certification and follow the code of conduct, including disclosure and suitability.
A distributor with a valid certificate offers a Category II fund.
Any person may distribute AIFs without certification.
Direct plan
AIFs must provide an option for investors to invest directly, without a distributor, and distribution commissions should be transparent.
An investor chooses to invest without paying a distributor.
AIFs may not be bought directly.
No public offering
AIFs cannot raise money through a public offer; they raise capital only by private placement.
A fund cannot advertise a public offer.
An AIF may issue an IPO for its units.
Disclosure and investor reporting
Managers must give investors periodic reports, including audited financials and NAV, within timelines set by SEBI.
A fund sends quarterly updates and an annual audit.
Managers need not report to investors.
Winding up
On the end of tenure, the fund must liquidate or distribute assets in specie, with approvals as required.
At term end, assets are sold or handed to investors.
A fund continues forever after the tenure ends.
Penalties
SEBI can penalise AIFs, managers and distributors for violations, including by suspension or cancellation.
A distributor is penalised for mis-selling an AIF.
SEBI has no power over AIF distributors.

units.title: AIF structuring
units.overview: Legal forms, fund-of-funds, feeders and who the parties to a fund are.
facts: Trust structure
Most AIFs are set up as trusts, with a trustee holding the fund's assets for investors as beneficiaries, giving flexibility and pass-through tax treatment.
A fund is a trust with a trustee and beneficiaries.
Most AIFs are public limited companies.
LLP and company forms
An AIF can also be set up as a limited liability partnership or a company, but trusts are the most common form.
A fund is structured as an LLP.
An AIF can only be a trust.
Sponsor
The sponsor is the person who sets up the AIF, and typically contributes capital and appoints the manager.
The firm that creates the fund and invests its own money.
The sponsor is an investor with no role in formation.
Investment manager
The investment manager manages the fund's portfolio and operations under an investment management agreement, earning fees.
A company makes the investment decisions of the fund.
The manager is an investor in the fund.
Trustee
The trustee holds the fund's assets in trust and is responsible for oversight and ensuring the fund follows its documents.
An entity ensures the trust deed is complied with.
The trustee decides which companies to invest in.
Fund of funds
A fund of funds invests in other AIFs rather than directly in companies, adding diversification but another layer of fees.
A Category II fund invests in several PE funds.
A fund of funds invests directly in start-ups.
Feeder fund
A feeder fund collects money from investors and invests it in a master fund, often used for foreign investors or to pool distributions.
A fund channels investor money into a larger master fund.
A feeder fund invests in listed shares only.
Scheme versus fund
An AIF can launch multiple schemes under one registration, each with its own investors, strategy and tenure.
A registered fund offers a new scheme every year.
An AIF can launch only one scheme.
Co-investment
Co-investment lets selected investors invest directly alongside the fund in a deal, often with lower fees, subject to regulatory conditions.
An investor is offered a direct stake in a deal alongside the fund.
Co-investment is prohibited.
GIFT City funds
Funds set up in GIFT City's IFSC can pool money in foreign currency and are governed by a separate regulatory framework.
A fund set up in the international financial centre raises dollar capital.
GIFT City funds are restricted to domestic rupee investing.
Pass-through
In a pass-through structure, income is taxed in the investors' hands rather than at the fund level, preserving the character of income.
Investors are taxed on the fund's capital gains directly.
Pass-through means the fund pays all the tax.
Side pocket
A side pocket separates illiquid or distressed assets from the main portfolio so that exits and fees of other investors are not affected.
A fund isolates a stuck investment for later realisation.
A side pocket merges all assets into one pool.

units.title: Risk and return: investor and fund perspective
units.overview: The risks specific to private funds, how returns are measured and what they depend on.
facts: Liquidity risk in AIFs
AIF investors cannot redeem on demand; capital is locked for the tenure and exit depends on the fund's realisations.
An investor needs cash but the fund has two more years to run.
AIF units can be redeemed any day.
Valuation risk
Unlisted assets are valued by models and judgement, so reported NAV can differ from realised value.
A fund's marked value drops when the asset is sold for less.
Valuation risk does not arise in private assets.
Concentration risk
AIFs often hold a small number of investments, so one failure can have a large impact on returns.
A fund with ten investments loses heavily when one fails.
AIFs are always well diversified across hundreds of assets.
Manager and key-person risk
Returns depend on the skill and continuity of the manager's team; the departure of key people can damage a fund.
A star investor leaves the fund house.
Manager risk does not matter for AIFs.
Leverage risk
Use of debt, at fund or investee level, amplifies gains and losses and may cause distress in downturns.
An investee with heavy debt struggles when rates rise.
Leverage lowers the risk of losses.
Exit risk
The returns of a private fund rely on exits via IPO, sale or buyback, which depend on market conditions and may be delayed.
A fund cannot list its investee because markets are weak.
Exit is guaranteed at the fund's tenure.
Regulatory and tax risk
Changes in law or tax treatment can reduce net returns or alter the structure.
A change in tax rules reduces after-tax returns.
Regulations never change for AIFs.
Return expectations
Alternatives aim to deliver higher returns than listed markets as compensation for illiquidity and risk, but outcomes vary widely.
A PE fund targets a premium over equity indices.
AIFs guarantee a return above listed markets.
Risk-adjusted performance
Because private assets are valued infrequently, volatility looks low; investors should look at drawdowns, dispersion and realised returns.
An advisor looks at realised returns instead of reported NAV smoothness.
Low reported volatility proves low risk.
Dispersion of returns
The difference between top and bottom funds is large in private markets, so manager selection matters more than in listed funds.
The best PE fund greatly outperforms the worst.
All funds in a category perform alike.
Fees and net returns
Management fees, carry and expenses reduce net returns, so investors compare returns after all costs.
A fund's gross multiple looks good but net is lower after fees.
Gross returns are what investors receive.
Concentration limits as risk control
Regulatory limits on single-investee exposure help to reduce concentration risk in Category I and II AIFs.
A fund cannot put more than 25% in one company.
There are no limits on a single investment.

units.title: Investment process and governance of funds
units.overview: How a fund finds, chooses, monitors and exits investments, and how it governs itself.
facts: Deal sourcing
Sourcing is how a manager finds investment opportunities, through networks, bankers and proprietary research.
A manager receives a deal from a banker.
Sourcing means selecting an auditor.
Screening
Screening filters opportunities against the fund's strategy, size, sector and risk criteria before detailed work begins.
A manager rejects deals outside its target sector.
Screening is the final approval of the investment.
Investee due diligence
The manager studies the investee's business, financials, legal and tax position and management before investing.
A fund examines the target company's books and contracts.
Due diligence is carried out only after the investment.
Investment committee
The investment committee reviews and approves investments, applying independent judgement and recording decisions.
A panel votes on each deal before funds are committed.
The committee approves only fees.
Term sheet
A term sheet sets the key terms of an investment, such as valuation, rights and conditions, before definitive agreements.
The manager and company agree the main terms in a short document.
A term sheet is the final legal agreement.
Active involvement
Many private funds take board seats and help investees with strategy, hiring and governance to create value.
A fund representative joins the investee's board.
Funds never engage with investees.
Monitoring investments
Managers track investee performance through reports, board meetings and key metrics, and intervene when needed.
A fund reviews monthly MIS from its investee.
Monitoring ends once money is invested.
Advisory committee
An advisory committee of investors reviews conflicts, valuations and other matters referred by the manager, giving investors a voice.
Investors on a committee approve related-party deals.
The committee manages day-to-day investments.
Conflict of interest policy
The manager must have a policy to identify, disclose and manage conflicts, such as allocating deals between funds.
A fund discloses how a deal is shared across its funds.
Conflicts of interest do not arise in private funds.
Key-person clause
A key-person clause suspends new investments if named individuals leave or devote less time, protecting investors.
The fund stops investing when the lead partner departs.
A key-person clause guarantees returns.
Allocation of investments
Managers should allocate opportunities fairly across funds and co-investors according to policy.
A deal is split among funds based on a stated allocation rule.
Managers may favour the fund where they earn the most fees.
Exit planning
Exit routes include IPO, strategic sale, secondary sale and buyback, and planning begins early in the investment.
A fund sells its stake to a larger company.
Exit planning begins after the fund term ends.

units.title: Fund due diligence: investor perspective
units.overview: The most important unit for a distributor: how to evaluate a fund before recommending it. Expect scenario questions.
facts: Fund due diligence
Due diligence is the investor's independent assessment of a fund and its manager before committing, covering people, process, performance, terms and operations.
A distributor reviews a fund thoroughly before recommending it to a client.
Due diligence is unnecessary if the fund is SEBI-registered.
Track record analysis
A manager's track record should be checked for realised returns, consistency, attribution and whether the team that earned it is still present.
An adviser reviews a manager's exits and the team behind them.
Only unrealised mark-ups should be considered.
Team stability
Stability and depth of the investment team, incentives and succession are critical to the fund's success.
A fund where senior members have left raises concerns.
Team changes have no effect on a fund.
Strategy fit
The fund's strategy should be clear, repeatable and consistent with the client's goals, risk appetite and horizon.
A fund's focus on late-stage companies is compared with the client's needs.
Any strategy suits any client.
Alignment of interest
Alignment is shown by meaningful manager commitment, performance-linked pay and fees that reward results rather than assets alone.
The manager invests a large sum of its own money.
Alignment means the manager has no money in the fund.
Fee review
Investors should review management fee, carry, hurdle, catch-up, expenses and clawback to understand their total cost.
A distributor compares the fee structures of two funds.
Only the management fee matters.
Operational due diligence
ODD examines back-office systems, valuation process, compliance, custody and controls to check that the manager can run the fund reliably.
A review of the fund's administrators, auditors and valuation policy.
Operational checks are not needed for good performers.
Legal due diligence
Legal DD reviews the offer documents, structure, regulatory standing and litigation to ensure investor protection.
A lawyer checks the trust deed and the PPM.
Legal review is only about taxes.
Reference checks
Speaking with existing investors, investee CEOs and co-investors gives independent views on the manager's conduct and value addition.
An adviser calls entrepreneurs the manager has backed.
References should be taken only from the manager.
Performance attribution
Attribution separates returns due to skill from those due to market conditions, leverage or one lucky investment.
An adviser checks whether one deal produced most of the gains.
Attribution is the same as total return.
Portfolio concentration review
Reviewing the fund's concentration by company, sector and vintage reveals risks of overexposure.
A fund has half its capital in one sector.
Concentration review is irrelevant for private funds.
Valuation policy review
Investors should check how the fund values holdings, how often, and who reviews valuations, to avoid inflated NAVs.
A fund uses an independent valuer under a documented policy.
Valuations can be set by the manager without any policy.
Red flags
Red flags include unclear strategy, no track record, excessive fees, weak controls, related-party deals, resistance to disclosure and promised returns.
A manager promises a return of 25% a year and refuses to share documents.
Promised high returns are a sign of safety.
Compliance and regulatory standing
Checking registration, past SEBI actions and compliance history helps assess the manager's integrity.
An adviser checks the manager's regulatory record.
Past regulatory actions are irrelevant.
Concentration of investor base
A fund dependent on one or two large investors may face redemption or governance pressure; diverse investors are generally healthier.
A fund where one investor holds most units.
A single large investor makes a fund safer.
Client suitability for AIFs
AIFs suit investors with surplus funds who can lock money for years and tolerate loss; not those needing liquidity.
A client needing money in two years is not a fit.
AIFs suit every client regardless of horizon.
Documentation of due diligence
Distributors should document the due diligence and reasons for recommending a fund, to evidence suitability.
A file records the checks made before recommending the fund.
Records of due diligence are unnecessary.
Ongoing manager review
Due diligence does not end at investment; monitoring continues through reports, meetings and performance reviews.
An adviser reviews the fund's quarterly report each time it arrives.
After investing, no further review is needed.

units.title: Legal documents and negotiations: investor perspective
units.overview: What documents govern an AIF investment and which clauses protect investors.
facts: Private placement memorandum
The PPM is the principal disclosure document describing the fund's strategy, terms, fees, risks and governance.
A prospective investor reads the PPM before signing.
The PPM is signed by the investor as a contract.
Contribution agreement
The contribution (or subscription) agreement is the contract in which the investor commits capital to the fund on set terms.
An investor signs to commit ₹3 crore under the fund's terms.
A contribution agreement is a loan agreement.
Trust deed
The trust deed sets up the fund as a trust, defining the roles of trustee, sponsor and manager, and the rights of beneficiaries.
A legal document creates the trust and sets its rules.
The trust deed is a marketing brochure.
Investment management agreement
The IMA appoints the manager and sets its duties, authority, fees and standards of care.
A contract between the trustee and the investment manager.
The IMA is an agreement among investors only.
Side letter
A side letter gives an individual investor special rights or terms, such as reporting or fee discounts, separate from the main documents.
A large investor negotiates a lower fee in a separate letter.
A side letter changes terms for all investors.
Most-favoured-nation clause
An MFN clause lets an investor elect the better terms granted to other investors in comparable side letters.
An investor opts for a lower fee granted to another investor.
An MFN clause gives the manager the best terms.
Default provisions
If an investor fails to meet a capital call, the fund can impose penalties, such as forfeiting part of the interest or reducing its holding.
A defaulting investor loses part of its stake.
Missing a capital call has no consequences.
No-fault removal
A no-fault removal clause lets investors remove the manager by a supermajority vote without proving misconduct.
Investors vote to replace the manager though no wrongdoing is alleged.
The manager can be removed only for fraud.
Indemnification
Indemnification clauses protect the manager from liability for acts in good faith but should exclude fraud, gross negligence and wilful default.
The manager is protected unless it acts fraudulently.
The manager is indemnified for fraud.
Distribution provisions
These set how and when proceeds are distributed, including the waterfall, reinvestment rights and in-specie distributions.
The fund pays investors in cash or in shares as per terms.
Distributions are at the manager's whim.
Term and extension
The term clause states the fund's life and the conditions under which it can be extended, normally needing investor approval.
A fund can extend by two years with the vote of investors.
The manager may extend the term at any time.
Investor transfer rights
The documents set conditions for transferring units, usually needing manager consent, as the fund is illiquid.
An investor needs approval to sell her units.
Units can be freely traded on exchanges.
Negotiating priorities
Investors, especially large ones, negotiate on fees, governance rights, reporting, key-person triggers and transfer terms.
An anchor investor seeks a seat on the advisory committee.
Investor terms cannot be negotiated.
Governing law and disputes
The documents specify governing law, jurisdiction and dispute resolution, often through arbitration.
Disputes go to arbitration in India as per the agreement.
Documents are silent on disputes.
Disclosures of risk factors
The PPM must list material risks; investors should read them and not rely on verbal assurances.
An investor relies on the written risk factors.
Verbal assurances override written documents.

units.title: Fund monitoring, reporting and exit
units.overview: Staying informed after investing and how exits return money.
facts: Investor reporting
Managers provide regular reports such as NAV, portfolio updates, audited accounts and notice of material events.
An investor receives a quarterly report with portfolio commentary.
Managers need not report until the end of the fund.
Capital account statement
A statement showing the investor's contributions, distributions, fees and current value.
An investor reads her statement of units and paid-in capital.
The statement shows the manager's personal investments.
IPO exit
An IPO lets the fund sell shares of an investee to the public after listing, often subject to lock-in.
A fund sells shares after the investee lists.
An IPO exit is not available to PE funds.
Strategic sale
A strategic sale transfers the investee to another company, often at a premium.
A larger company buys the investee outright.
A strategic sale is a stock market listing.
Secondary sale
A secondary sale transfers the fund's stake to another financial investor, such as another PE fund.
A fund sells its stake to a different investment fund.
A secondary sale is the fund's first investment.
Buyback by promoter
In a promoter buyback, the founders repurchase the fund's stake, often at a pre-agreed return.
The founders buy out the fund's stake.
A promoter buyback is a new fundraising.
In-specie distribution
In-specie distribution gives investors the underlying securities instead of cash when the fund winds up or at exit.
An investor receives listed shares instead of cash.
In-specie means paying in foreign currency.
Winding up
On termination the fund realises or distributes remaining assets, settles liabilities and returns proceeds per the waterfall.
At the end of term the trust is closed and assets are paid out.
Winding up leaves investors' capital with the manager.

units.title: Valuation
units.overview: How private assets are valued and why it matters for NAV and fees.
facts: Fair value
Fair value is the price at which an asset could be sold in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date.
A fund estimates what an unlisted holding would fetch in a sale today.
Fair value equals the purchase cost always.
Discounted cash flow
DCF values an asset as the present value of expected future cash flows.
A valuer projects future cash flows and discounts them.
DCF uses only the last transaction price.
Comparable multiples
This method values a company using multiples such as EV/EBITDA of similar listed firms, adjusted for size and liquidity.
A valuer applies peers' EV/EBITDA to the investee's earnings.
Comparable multiples need no peer companies.
Last round price
The price of a recent funding round is a data point for fair value, but it may need adjustment if conditions change.
A start-up is valued by its latest financing.
The last round price is always right.
Cost basis
Valuing at cost is acceptable only for a short period after investment, until better evidence is available.
A newly bought stake is held at cost for a while.
Cost is the right basis for old investments.
Independent valuer
SEBI requires valuation of an AIF's investments by an independent valuer for certain funds, and valuation should be done at regular intervals.
An independent firm values the portfolio every half year.
The manager alone may value its holdings.
IPEV guidelines
The International Private Equity and Venture Capital valuation guidelines are a widely used standard for valuing private holdings.
A fund follows a global standard for valuation.
IPEV guidelines apply to listed shares.
Valuation and fees
Because fees can depend on NAV or invested capital, inflated valuations can overstate performance and fees, so independent checks matter.
An inflated NAV can raise a manager's fee.
Valuation has no link to fees.

units.title: Taxation: India specific
units.overview: How AIFs and their investors are taxed.
focus: Pass-through for Category I and II.
facts: Pass-through status
Category I and II AIFs enjoy pass-through status: income other than business income is taxed in the investors' hands, retaining its character.
Capital gains of the fund are taxed in the investor's hands.
Category II AIFs pay tax on all income at the fund level.
Business income of AIF
Business income earned by a Category I or II AIF is taxed at the fund level and is not passed through.
A fund's trading business profit is taxed at the fund.
All fund income is taxed in the investor's hands.
Category III taxation
Category III AIFs do not get pass-through status in the same way; income is generally taxed at the fund level as per the Act.
A hedge fund's profits are taxed within the fund.
Category III AIFs are fully pass-through.
Character retained
Because of pass-through, gains retain their nature, such as long-term capital gains, when taxed in the investor's hands.
A long-term gain in the fund remains long-term for the investor.
Gains lose their character after passing through.
TDS on distributions

Fair value is the price at which an asset could be sold in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date.
Fair value equals the purchase cost always.
mocks.w: Correct: Fair value is the price at which an asset could be sold in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Ongoing manager review” is correct?
o: After investing, no further review is needed.
Units can be freely traded on exchanges.
The manager alone may value its holdings.
Due diligence does not end at investment; monitoring continues through reports, meetings and performance reviews.
mocks.w: Correct: Due diligence does not end at investment; monitoring continues through reports, meetings and performance reviews.

mocks.p: Which term is described here? A secondary sale transfers the fund's stake to another financial investor, such as another PE fund.
o: Hurdle rate
Secondary sale
Minimum corpus
Vintage year
mocks.w: Secondary sale: A secondary sale transfers the fund's stake to another financial investor, such as another PE fund.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Leverage risk” is correct?
o: Leverage lowers the risk of losses.
A strategic sale is a stock market listing.
Use of debt, at fund or investee level, amplifies gains and losses and may cause distress in downturns.
Hedge funds can only buy and hold equities.
mocks.w: Correct: Use of debt, at fund or investee level, amplifies gains and losses and may cause distress in downturns.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Key-person clause” is correct?
o: A key-person clause guarantees returns.
SEBI has no power over AIF distributors.
A key-person clause suspends new investments if named individuals leave or devote less time, protecting investors.
Vintage year is the year of exit.
mocks.w: Correct: A key-person clause suspends new investments if named individuals leave or devote less time, protecting investors.

mocks.p: Which statement best describes “Co-investment”?
o: AIFs must provide an option for investors to invest directly, without a distributor, and distribution commissions should be transparent.
Attribution separates returns due to skill from those due to market conditions, leverage or one lucky investment.
The contribution (or subscription) agreement is the contract in which the investor commits capital to the fund on set terms.
Co-investment lets selected investors invest directly alongside the fund in a deal, often with lower fees, subject to regulatory conditions.
mocks.w: Co-investment: Co-investment lets selected investors invest directly alongside the fund in a deal, often with lower fees, subject to regulatory conditions.

mocks.p: Which term is described here? SEBI can penalise AIFs, managers and distributors for violations, including by suspension or cancellation.
o: Investor transfer rights
Penalties
Reference checks
Red flags
mocks.w: Penalties: SEBI can penalise AIFs, managers and distributors for violations, including by suspension or cancellation.

mocks.p: Which term is described here? An advisory committee of investors reviews conflicts, valuations and other matters referred by the manager, giving investors a voice.
o: General partner and limited partner
Advisory committee
Clawback
Concentration of investor base
mocks.w: Advisory committee: An advisory committee of investors reviews conflicts, valuations and other matters referred by the manager, giving investors a voice.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Manager and key-person risk” is correct?
o: The committee manages day-to-day investments.
Returns depend on the skill and continuity of the manager's team; the departure of key people can damage a fund.
AIF units can be redeemed any day.
Manager risk does not matter for AIFs.
mocks.w: Correct: Returns depend on the skill and continuity of the manager's team; the departure of key people can damage a fund.

mocks.p: Which term is described here? A side letter gives an individual investor special rights or terms, such as reporting or fee discounts, separate from the main documents.
o: Independent valuer
Alignment of interest
Side letter
LLP and company forms
mocks.w: Side letter: A side letter gives an individual investor special rights or terms, such as reporting or fee discounts, separate from the main documents.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Trust structure” is correct?
o: Regulations never change for AIFs.
Most AIFs are public limited companies.
Most AIFs are set up as trusts, with a trustee holding the fund's assets for investors as beneficiaries, giving flexibility and pass-through tax treatment.
An AIF can start raising money before registration.
mocks.w: Correct: Most AIFs are set up as trusts, with a trustee holding the fund's assets for investors as beneficiaries, giving flexibility and pass-through tax treatment.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Strategy fit” is correct?
o: Venture capital funds only mature, stable firms.
Private equity invests only in listed companies.
The fund's strategy should be clear, repeatable and consistent with the client's goals, risk appetite and horizon.
Any strategy suits any client.
mocks.w: Correct: The fund's strategy should be clear, repeatable and consistent with the client's goals, risk appetite and horizon.

mocks.p: Which term is described here? Returns from alternatives depend heavily on manager skill, so dispersion between top and bottom managers is wide.
o: Sponsor and manager commitment
Category III taxation
Disclosures of risk factors
Manager skill
mocks.w: Manager skill: Returns from alternatives depend heavily on manager skill, so dispersion between top and bottom managers is wide.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Business income of AIF” is correct?
o: Team changes have no effect on a fund.
Business income earned by a Category I or II AIF is taxed at the fund level and is not passed through.
All fund income is taxed in the investor's hands.
An AIF can only be a trust.
mocks.w: Correct: Business income earned by a Category I or II AIF is taxed at the fund level and is not passed through.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Contribution agreement” is correct?
o: The contribution (or subscription) agreement is the contract in which the investor commits capital to the fund on set terms.
A fund continues forever after the tenure ends.
A contribution agreement is a loan agreement.
GST is not applicable on any fee.
mocks.w: Correct: The contribution (or subscription) agreement is the contract in which the investor commits capital to the fund on set terms.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Regulatory and tax risk” is correct?
o: Regulations never change for AIFs.
Changes in law or tax treatment can reduce net returns or alter the structure.
A side pocket merges all assets into one pool.
Exit planning begins after the fund term ends.
mocks.w: Correct: Changes in law or tax treatment can reduce net returns or alter the structure.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Investment management agreement” is correct?
o: The IMA is an agreement among investors only.
LPs manage the fund's day-to-day investments.
The IMA appoints the manager and sets its duties, authority, fees and standards of care.
Funds never engage with investees.
mocks.w: Correct: The IMA appoints the manager and sets its duties, authority, fees and standards of care.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Fund due diligence” is correct?
o: Due diligence is unnecessary if the fund is SEBI-registered.
Most AIFs are public limited companies.
Due diligence is the investor's independent assessment of a fund and its manager before committing, covering people, process, performance, terms and operations.
Private funds show high returns from the first year.
mocks.w: Correct: Due diligence is the investor's independent assessment of a fund and its manager before committing, covering people, process, performance, terms and operations.

mocks.p: Which term is described here? Tax is deducted at source on income distributed to investors by pass-through AIFs at the rates prescribed, with credit available to the investor.
o: TDS on distributions
Illiquidity
Suitability
Capital account statement
mocks.w: TDS on distributions: Tax is deducted at source on income distributed to investors by pass-through AIFs at the rates prescribed, with credit available to the investor.

mocks.p: Which statement best describes “Disclosure and investor reporting”?
o: This method values a company using multiples such as EV/EBITDA of similar listed firms, adjusted for size and liquidity.
Category I and II AIFs may not invest more than 25% of investable funds in one investee company.
Managers must give investors periodic reports, including audited financials and NAV, within timelines set by SEBI.
Exit routes include IPO, strategic sale, secondary sale and buyback, and planning begins early in the investment.
mocks.w: Disclosure and investor reporting: Managers must give investors periodic reports, including audited financials and NAV, within timelines set by SEBI.

mocks.p: Which statement best describes “Discounted cash flow”?
o: DCF values an asset as the present value of expected future cash flows.
Investors should check how the fund values holdings, how often, and who reviews valuations, to avoid inflated NAVs.
A clawback requires the manager to return excess carry if, over the fund's life, it received more than its entitled share.
Changes in law or tax treatment can reduce net returns or alter the structure.
mocks.w: Discounted cash flow: DCF values an asset as the present value of expected future cash flows.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Angel fund” is correct?
o: Investor terms cannot be negotiated.
An angel fund invests in listed blue-chips.
An angel fund is a sub-category of Category I that pools money from angel investors to invest in early-stage start-ups, with smaller minimums.
An AIF raises money from the general public.
mocks.w: Correct: An angel fund is a sub-category of Category I that pools money from angel investors to invest in early-stage start-ups, with smaller minimums.

mocks.p: Which statement best describes “Documentation of due diligence”?
o: A no-fault removal clause lets investors remove the manager by a supermajority vote without proving misconduct.
Distributors should document the due diligence and reasons for recommending a fund, to evidence suitability.
In-specie distribution gives investors the underlying securities instead of cash when the fund winds up or at exit.
An IPO lets the fund sell shares of an investee to the public after listing, often subject to lock-in.
mocks.w: Documentation of due diligence: Distributors should document the due diligence and reasons for recommending a fund, to evidence suitability.

mocks.p: Which statement best describes “Winding up”?
o: On the end of tenure, the fund must liquidate or distribute assets in specie, with approvals as required.
The returns of a private fund rely on exits via IPO, sale or buyback, which depend on market conditions and may be delayed.
In a promoter buyback, the founders repurchase the fund's stake, often at a pre-agreed return.
Distributors should maintain records of recommendations, risk profiling, disclosures and communication for the period required.
mocks.w: Winding up: On the end of tenure, the fund must liquidate or distribute assets in specie, with approvals as required.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Category III AIF” is correct?
o: Category III AIFs cannot use leverage.
The last round price is always right.
An AIF raises money from the general public.
Category III AIFs, such as hedge funds, employ diverse or complex trading strategies and may use leverage and trade listed derivatives.
mocks.w: Correct: Category III AIFs, such as hedge funds, employ diverse or complex trading strategies and may use leverage and trade listed derivatives.

mocks.p: Which term is described here? Sourcing is how a manager finds investment opportunities, through networks, bankers and proprietary research.
o: Commission disclosure
Deal sourcing
Minimum corpus
No guaranteed returns
mocks.w: Deal sourcing: Sourcing is how a manager finds investment opportunities, through networks, bankers and proprietary research.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Pass-through status” is correct?
o: Category I and II AIFs enjoy pass-through status: income other than business income is taxed in the investors' hands, retaining its character.
Category II AIFs pay tax on all income at the fund level.
A secondary sale is the fund's first investment.
Funds never engage with investees.
mocks.w: Correct: Category I and II AIFs enjoy pass-through status: income other than business income is taxed in the investors' hands, retaining its character.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Monitoring investments” is correct?
o: Monitoring ends once money is invested.
Sponsors need not invest in the AIF.
Suitability applies only to mutual funds.
Managers track investee performance through reports, board meetings and key metrics, and intervene when needed.
mocks.w: Correct: Managers track investee performance through reports, board meetings and key metrics, and intervene when needed.

mocks.p: Which term is described here? Many private funds take board seats and help investees with strategy, hiring and governance to create value.
o: Exit risk
Category III AIF
Leverage risk
Active involvement
mocks.w: Active involvement: Many private funds take board seats and help investees with strategy, hiring and governance to create value.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Clawback” is correct?
o: A distributor should recommend the highest-commission fund.
A clawback lets managers keep any carry paid.
A clawback requires the manager to return excess carry if, over the fund's life, it received more than its entitled share.
IPEV guidelines apply to listed shares.
mocks.w: Correct: A clawback requires the manager to return excess carry if, over the fund's life, it received more than its entitled share.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Exit planning” is correct?
o: Alternatives offer daily redemption.
Exit routes include IPO, strategic sale, secondary sale and buyback, and planning begins early in the investment.
Exit planning begins after the fund term ends.
A single large investor makes a fund safer.
mocks.w: Correct: Exit routes include IPO, strategic sale, secondary sale and buyback, and planning begins early in the investment.

mocks.p: Which statement best describes “Client suitability for AIFs”?
o: Managers track investee performance through reports, board meetings and key metrics, and intervene when needed.
Distributors should not provide tax advice beyond their remit; investors should consult a tax professional.
Investors should check how the fund values holdings, how often, and who reviews valuations, to avoid inflated NAVs.
AIFs suit investors with surplus funds who can lock money for years and tolerate loss; not those needing liquidity.
mocks.w: Client suitability for AIFs: AIFs suit investors with surplus funds who can lock money for years and tolerate loss; not those needing liquidity.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Buyback by promoter” is correct?
o: Exit is guaranteed at the fund's tenure.
A promoter buyback is a new fundraising.
Sponsors need not invest in the AIF.
In a promoter buyback, the founders repurchase the fund's stake, often at a pre-agreed return.
mocks.w: Correct: In a promoter buyback, the founders repurchase the fund's stake, often at a pre-agreed return.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Number of investors” is correct?
o: An AIF scheme cannot have more than 1,000 investors (200 for angel funds) as it raises money through private placement.
Gross returns are what investors receive.
A distributor should recommend the highest-commission fund.
An AIF can have unlimited investors.
mocks.w: Correct: An AIF scheme cannot have more than 1,000 investors (200 for angel funds) as it raises money through private placement.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Private placement memorandum” is correct?
o: Commissions need not be disclosed.
The PPM is the offer document of an AIF, filed with SEBI through a merchant banker, describing strategy, fees, risks and terms.
The PPM is not required for AIFs.
DCF uses only the last transaction price.
mocks.w: Correct: The PPM is the offer document of an AIF, filed with SEBI through a merchant banker, describing strategy, fees, risks and terms.

mocks.p: Which term is described here? Category I AIFs invest in start-ups, early-stage ventures, SMEs, social ventures and infrastructure that the government considers socially or economically desirable.
o: Independent valuer
Category I AIF
Investments in associates
TDS on distributions
mocks.w: Category I AIF: Category I AIFs invest in start-ups, early-stage ventures, SMEs, social ventures and infrastructure that the government considers socially or economically desirable.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Portfolio concentration review” is correct?
o: Reviewing the fund's concentration by company, sector and vintage reveals risks of overexposure.
Alternatives always move exactly with equities.
The minimum investment is ₹10,000.
Concentration review is irrelevant for private funds.
mocks.w: Correct: Reviewing the fund's concentration by company, sector and vintage reveals risks of overexposure.

mocks.p: Which term is described here? Investments in associates and the manager's related parties need to be disclosed and approved by investors as per the regulations.
o: Liquidity risk in AIFs
Concentration limits as risk control
Investments in associates
Valuation risk
mocks.w: Investments in associates: Investments in associates and the manager's related parties need to be disclosed and approved by investors as per the regulations.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Feeder fund” is correct?
o: A feeder fund collects money from investors and invests it in a master fund, often used for foreign investors or to pool distributions.
The committee manages day-to-day investments.
A feeder fund invests in listed shares only.
Distributions are at the manager's whim.
mocks.w: Correct: A feeder fund collects money from investors and invests it in a master fund, often used for foreign investors or to pool distributions.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Custodian” is correct?
o: IPEV guidelines apply to listed shares.
AIFs hold securities with no custodian.
AIFs are required to appoint a custodian to safekeep their securities, as mandated by SEBI.
Exit is guaranteed at the fund's tenure.
mocks.w: Correct: AIFs are required to appoint a custodian to safekeep their securities, as mandated by SEBI.

mocks.p: Which term is described here? A catch-up lets the manager receive a larger share of distributions after the hurdle until it has received its full carry percentage of total profits.
o: Low correlation
Investment management agreement
Penalties
Catch-up
mocks.w: Catch-up: A catch-up lets the manager receive a larger share of distributions after the hurdle until it has received its full carry percentage of total profits.

mocks.p: Which statement best describes “Private equity”?
o: A key-person clause suspends new investments if named individuals leave or devote less time, protecting investors.
An MFN clause lets an investor elect the better terms granted to other investors in comparable side letters.
The sponsor is the person who sets up the AIF, and typically contributes capital and appoints the manager.
Private equity invests in unlisted companies, usually taking significant ownership, with the aim of growing value and exiting later.
mocks.w: Private equity: Private equity invests in unlisted companies, usually taking significant ownership, with the aim of growing value and exiting later.

mocks.p: Which statement best describes “Registration”?
o: Category I and II AIFs may not invest more than 25% of investable funds in one investee company.
An AIF must be registered with SEBI under one of the three categories before it raises funds.
If an investor fails to meet a capital call, the fund can impose penalties, such as forfeiting part of the interest or reducing its holding.
Because fees can depend on NAV or invested capital, inflated valuations can overstate performance and fees, so independent checks matter.
mocks.w: Registration: An AIF must be registered with SEBI under one of the three categories before it raises funds.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Disclosure to investors” is correct?
o: A distributor must give investors the PPM and explain risks, fees, lock-in and illiquidity before they invest.
AIFs are outside SEBI's regulation.
All fund income is taxed in the investor's hands.
Risk factors can be skipped if the client is wealthy.
mocks.w: Correct: A distributor must give investors the PPM and explain risks, fees, lock-in and illiquidity before they invest.

mocks.p: Which statement about “SEBI AIF Regulations 2012” is correct?
o: These regulations govern registration, investment conditions, disclosure and operation of AIFs in India.
AIFs are outside SEBI's regulation.
Operational checks are not needed for good performers.
AIFs never deduct TDS.
mocks.w: Correct: These regulations govern registration, investment conditions, disclosure and operation of AIFs in India.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Independent valuer” is correct?
o: Units can be freely traded on exchanges.
SEBI requires valuation of an AIF's investments by an independent valuer for certain funds, and valuation should be done at regular intervals.
The manager alone may value its holdings.
The trust deed is a marketing brochure.
mocks.w: Correct: SEBI requires valuation of an AIF's investments by an independent valuer for certain funds, and valuation should be done at regular intervals.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Venture capital” is correct?
o: Venture capital funds only mature, stable firms.
Venture capital funds early-stage, high-growth companies, accepting high failure rates for the chance of outsized returns.
An AIF can start with any amount.
Most AIFs are public limited companies.
mocks.w: Correct: Venture capital funds early-stage, high-growth companies, accepting high failure rates for the chance of outsized returns.

mocks.p: Which statement about “DPI, RVPI and TVPI” is correct?
o: DPI is distributions divided by paid-in capital, RVPI is residual value divided by paid-in capital, and TVPI is their sum.
Category II AIFs pay tax on all income at the fund level.
Exit is guaranteed at the fund's tenure.
DPI includes unrealised value.
mocks.w: Correct: DPI is distributions divided by paid-in capital, RVPI is residual value divided by paid-in capital, and TVPI is their sum.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Fees and net returns” is correct?
o: Management fees, carry and expenses reduce net returns, so investors compare returns after all costs.
Conflicts of interest do not arise in private funds.
The hurdle rate is the management fee.
Gross returns are what investors receive.
mocks.w: Correct: Management fees, carry and expenses reduce net returns, so investors compare returns after all costs.

mocks.p: Which term is described here? Distributors must avoid or disclose conflicts, such as higher commission on a product, and put client interest first.
o: Conflicts of interest
Portfolio concentration review
Fair value
In-specie distribution
mocks.w: Conflicts of interest: Distributors must avoid or disclose conflicts, such as higher commission on a product, and put client interest first.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Scheme versus fund” is correct?
o: A clawback lets managers keep any carry paid.
An AIF can launch only one scheme.
A feeder fund invests in listed shares only.
An AIF can launch multiple schemes under one registration, each with its own investors, strategy and tenure.
mocks.w: Correct: An AIF can launch multiple schemes under one registration, each with its own investors, strategy and tenure.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Alternative investments” is correct?
o: The statement shows the manager's personal investments.
Alternative investments are assets other than listed equity, bonds and cash, such as private equity, venture capital, hedge funds, real estate and infrastructure.
Alternative investments are the same as listed shares.
A strategic sale is a stock market listing.
mocks.w: Correct: Alternative investments are assets other than listed equity, bonds and cash, such as private equity, venture capital, hedge funds, real estate and infrastructure.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Valuation risk” is correct?
o: The trustee decides which companies to invest in.
Unlisted assets are valued by models and judgement, so reported NAV can differ from realised value.
Valuation risk does not arise in private assets.
Exit planning begins after the fund term ends.
mocks.w: Correct: Unlisted assets are valued by models and judgement, so reported NAV can differ from realised value.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Valuation and fees” is correct?
o: Because fees can depend on NAV or invested capital, inflated valuations can overstate performance and fees, so independent checks matter.
Valuation has no link to fees.
Risk factors can be skipped if the client is wealthy.
Only unrealised mark-ups should be considered.
mocks.w: Correct: Because fees can depend on NAV or invested capital, inflated valuations can overstate performance and fees, so independent checks matter.

mocks.p: Which term is described here? The documents specify governing law, jurisdiction and dispute resolution, often through arbitration.
o: Client suitability for AIFs
Scheme versus fund
Governing law and disputes
Benchmarking and reporting
mocks.w: Governing law and disputes: The documents specify governing law, jurisdiction and dispute resolution, often through arbitration.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Investment committee” is correct?
o: An AIF can only be a trust.
The PPM is signed by the investor as a contract.
The committee approves only fees.
The investment committee reviews and approves investments, applying independent judgement and recording decisions.
mocks.w: Correct: The investment committee reviews and approves investments, applying independent judgement and recording decisions.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Red flags” is correct?
o: The trustee decides which companies to invest in.
Red flags include unclear strategy, no track record, excessive fees, weak controls, related-party deals, resistance to disclosure and promised returns.
Regulations never change for AIFs.
Promised high returns are a sign of safety.
mocks.w: Correct: Red flags include unclear strategy, no track record, excessive fees, weak controls, related-party deals, resistance to disclosure and promised returns.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Legal due diligence” is correct?
o: An AIF can launch only one scheme.
Legal DD reviews the offer documents, structure, regulatory standing and litigation to ensure investor protection.
Monitoring ends once money is invested.
Legal review is only about taxes.
mocks.w: Correct: Legal DD reviews the offer documents, structure, regulatory standing and litigation to ensure investor protection.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Compliance and regulatory standing” is correct?
o: Checking registration, past SEBI actions and compliance history helps assess the manager's integrity.
Past regulatory actions are irrelevant.
Monitoring ends once money is invested.
Category II AIFs may leverage up to 5 times.
mocks.w: Correct: Checking registration, past SEBI actions and compliance history helps assess the manager's integrity.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Return expectations” is correct?
o: Alternatives aim to deliver higher returns than listed markets as compensation for illiquidity and risk, but outcomes vary widely.
Legal review is only about taxes.
The committee approves only fees.
AIFs guarantee a return above listed markets.
mocks.w: Correct: Alternatives aim to deliver higher returns than listed markets as compensation for illiquidity and risk, but outcomes vary widely.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Sponsor” is correct?
o: The sponsor is the person who sets up the AIF, and typically contributes capital and appoints the manager.
AIFs are always well diversified across hundreds of assets.
The committee manages day-to-day investments.
The sponsor is an investor with no role in formation.
mocks.w: Correct: The sponsor is the person who sets up the AIF, and typically contributes capital and appoints the manager.

mocks.p: Which term is described here? Stability and depth of the investment team, incentives and succession are critical to the fund's success.
o: Team stability
Most-favoured-nation clause
GST on fees
Leverage risk
mocks.w: Team stability: Stability and depth of the investment team, incentives and succession are critical to the fund's success.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Hedge fund strategies” is correct?
o: Screening is the final approval of the investment.
Hedge funds use strategies such as long-short, market-neutral, event-driven and macro, often with leverage and derivatives.
Hedge funds can only buy and hold equities.
AIFs never deduct TDS.
mocks.w: Correct: Hedge funds use strategies such as long-short, market-neutral, event-driven and macro, often with leverage and derivatives.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Concentration limits as risk control” is correct?
o: There are no limits on a single investment.
An AIF can only be a trust.
Most AIFs are public limited companies.
Regulatory limits on single-investee exposure help to reduce concentration risk in Category I and II AIFs.
mocks.w: Correct: Regulatory limits on single-investee exposure help to reduce concentration risk in Category I and II AIFs.

mocks.p: Which statement best describes “GST on fees”?
o: AIFs are required to appoint a custodian to safekeep their securities, as mandated by SEBI.
Management fees and certain charges to the fund may attract goods and services tax, affecting net returns.
The J-curve describes how returns in a private fund are negative in early years due to fees and unrealised investments, then rise as investments mature and exit.
Managers should allocate opportunities fairly across funds and co-investors according to policy.
mocks.w: GST on fees: Management fees and certain charges to the fund may attract goods and services tax, affecting net returns.

mocks.p: Which statement best describes “Risk-adjusted performance”?
o: A side letter gives an individual investor special rights or terms, such as reporting or fee discounts, separate from the main documents.
The hurdle rate or preferred return is the minimum return investors must receive before the manager earns carry.
Because private assets are valued infrequently, volatility looks low; investors should look at drawdowns, dispersion and realised returns.
A feeder fund collects money from investors and invests it in a master fund, often used for foreign investors or to pool distributions.
mocks.w: Risk-adjusted performance: Because private assets are valued infrequently, volatility looks low; investors should look at drawdowns, dispersion and realised returns.

mocks.p: Which term is described here? Attribution separates returns due to skill from those due to market conditions, leverage or one lucky investment.
o: Discounted cash flow
Performance attribution
Feeder fund
Most-favoured-nation clause
mocks.w: Performance attribution: Attribution separates returns due to skill from those due to market conditions, leverage or one lucky investment.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Management fee” is correct?
o: The last round price is always right.
AIFs suit every client regardless of horizon.
The management fee is a yearly percentage of commitments or invested capital charged to cover the manager's operating costs, regardless of performance.
The management fee is paid only on profits.
mocks.w: Correct: The management fee is a yearly percentage of commitments or invested capital charged to cover the manager's operating costs, regardless of performance.

mocks.p: Which term is described here? A manager's track record should be checked for realised returns, consistency, attribution and whether the team that earned it is still present.
o: Investee due diligence
Monitoring investments
Track record analysis
Pass-through status
mocks.w: Track record analysis: A manager's track record should be checked for realised returns, consistency, attribution and whether the team that earned it is still present.

mocks.p: Which statement best describes “Penalties”?
o: IRR measures annualised return accounting for timing of flows; MOIC is total value divided by invested capital, ignoring time.
Sponsor or manager must invest in the fund as 'skin in the game': 2.5% of the corpus or ₹5 crore, whichever is lower, for Category I and II.
SEBI can penalise AIFs, managers and distributors for violations, including by suspension or cancellation.
Investors should review management fee, carry, hurdle, catch-up, expenses and clawback to understand their total cost.
mocks.w: Penalties: SEBI can penalise AIFs, managers and distributors for violations, including by suspension or cancellation.

mocks.p: Which statement about “LLP and company forms” is correct?
o: Leverage lowers the risk of losses.
An AIF can also be set up as a limited liability partnership or a company, but trusts are the most common form.
An AIF can only be a trust.
Team changes have no effect on a fund.
mocks.w: Correct: An AIF can also be set up as a limited liability partnership or a company, but trusts are the most common form.

mocks.p: Which statement best describes “Disclosures of risk factors”?
o: The PPM must list material risks; investors should read them and not rely on verbal assurances.
AIFs must report performance to benchmarking agencies recognised by SEBI, supporting comparability and transparency.
These set how and when proceeds are distributed, including the waterfall, reinvestment rights and in-specie distributions.
An AIF can also be set up as a limited liability partnership or a company, but trusts are the most common form.
mocks.w: Disclosures of risk factors: The PPM must list material risks; investors should read them and not rely on verbal assurances.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Documentation of due diligence” is correct?
o: Distributors should document the due diligence and reasons for recommending a fund, to evidence suitability.
Records of due diligence are unnecessary.
Comparable multiples need no peer companies.
Valuation has no link to fees.
mocks.w: Correct: Distributors should document the due diligence and reasons for recommending a fund, to evidence suitability.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Confidentiality” is correct?
o: Client data may be sold to fund managers.
A Category II AIF may invest all funds in one company.
A distributor must protect client information and share it only with consent or as required by law.
Funds never engage with investees.
mocks.w: Correct: A distributor must protect client information and share it only with consent or as required by law.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Strategic sale” is correct?
o: Carried interest is paid before investors get their capital back.
A strategic sale is a stock market listing.
Valuation risk does not arise in private assets.
A strategic sale transfers the investee to another company, often at a premium.
mocks.w: Correct: A strategic sale transfers the investee to another company, often at a premium.

mocks.p: Which statement about “IPO exit” is correct?
o: An IPO lets the fund sell shares of an investee to the public after listing, often subject to lock-in.
Due diligence is carried out only after the investment.
Sourcing means selecting an auditor.
An IPO exit is not available to PE funds.
mocks.w: Correct: An IPO lets the fund sell shares of an investee to the public after listing, often subject to lock-in.

mocks.p: A change in tax rules reduces after-tax returns. Which idea does this illustrate?
o: Exit risk
Return expectations
Dispersion of returns
Regulatory and tax risk
mocks.w: This is Regulatory and tax risk. Changes in law or tax treatment can reduce net returns or alter the structure.

mocks.p: A fund reviews monthly MIS from its investee. Which idea does this illustrate?
o: Exit planning
Monitoring investments
Conflict of interest policy
Investment committee
mocks.w: This is Monitoring investments. Managers track investee performance through reports, board meetings and key metrics, and intervene when needed.

mocks.p: A distributor discloses that one fund pays more and recommends the better fit. Which idea does this illustrate?
o: Disclosure to investors
Commission disclosure
Conflicts of interest
Record keeping
mocks.w: This is Conflicts of interest. Distributors must avoid or disclose conflicts, such as higher commission on a product, and put client interest first.

mocks.p: A valuer applies peers' EV/EBITDA to the investee's earnings. Which idea does this illustrate?
o: Independent valuer
Discounted cash flow
Comparable multiples
Last round price
mocks.w: This is Comparable multiples. This method values a company using multiples such as EV/EBITDA of similar listed firms, adjusted for size and liquidity.

mocks.p: An investor needs approval to sell her units. Which idea does this illustrate?
o: Term and extension
Distribution provisions
Side letter
Investor transfer rights
mocks.w: This is Investor transfer rights. The documents set conditions for transferring units, usually needing manager consent, as the fund is illiquid.

mocks.p: A manager rejects deals outside its target sector. Which idea does this illustrate?
o: Investment committee
Term sheet
Advisory committee
Screening
mocks.w: This is Screening. Screening filters opportunities against the fund's strategy, size, sector and risk criteria before detailed work begins.

mocks.p: A long-term gain in the fund remains long-term for the investor. Which idea does this illustrate?
o: Category III taxation
Pass-through status
GST on fees
Character retained
mocks.w: This is Character retained. Because of pass-through, gains retain their nature, such as long-term capital gains, when taxed in the investor's hands.

mocks.p: A file records the checks made before recommending the fund. Which idea does this illustrate?
o: Documentation of due diligence
Operational due diligence
Valuation policy review
Team stability
mocks.w: This is Documentation of due diligence. Distributors should document the due diligence and reasons for recommending a fund, to evidence suitability.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Category III taxation” is correct?
o: Distributors should give detailed tax opinions.
All fund income is taxed in the investor's hands.
Category III AIFs do not get pass-through status in the same way; income is generally taxed at the fund level as per the Act.
Category III AIFs are fully pass-through.
mocks.w: Correct: Category III AIFs do not get pass-through status in the same way; income is generally taxed at the fund level as per the Act.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Direct plan” is correct?
o: Managers need not report to investors.
AIFs may not be bought directly.
AIFs must provide an option for investors to invest directly, without a distributor, and distribution commissions should be transparent.
A Category II AIF may invest all funds in one company.
mocks.w: Correct: AIFs must provide an option for investors to invest directly, without a distributor, and distribution commissions should be transparent.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Deal sourcing” is correct?
o: The committee manages day-to-day investments.
The committee approves only fees.
Sourcing is how a manager finds investment opportunities, through networks, bankers and proprietary research.
Sourcing means selecting an auditor.
mocks.w: Correct: Sourcing is how a manager finds investment opportunities, through networks, bankers and proprietary research.

mocks.p: A fee invoice carries GST. Which idea does this illustrate?
o: Tax planning limits
Category III taxation
Character retained
GST on fees
mocks.w: This is GST on fees. Management fees and certain charges to the fund may attract goods and services tax, affecting net returns.

mocks.p: A PE fund targets a premium over equity indices. Which idea does this illustrate?
o: Return expectations
Concentration limits as risk control
Risk-adjusted performance
Manager and key-person risk
mocks.w: This is Return expectations. Alternatives aim to deliver higher returns than listed markets as compensation for illiquidity and risk, but outcomes vary widely.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Track record analysis” is correct?
o: Only unrealised mark-ups should be considered.
Any strategy suits any client.
Due diligence is unnecessary if the fund is SEBI-registered.
A manager's track record should be checked for realised returns, consistency, attribution and whether the team that earned it is still present.
mocks.w: Correct: A manager's track record should be checked for realised returns, consistency, attribution and whether the team that earned it is still present.

mocks.p: A scheme caps its investor count at 1,000. Which idea does this illustrate?
o: Category III AIF
Accredited investor
Alternative Investment Fund
Number of investors
mocks.w: This is Number of investors. An AIF scheme cannot have more than 1,000 investors (200 for angel funds) as it raises money through private placement.

mocks.p: A fund has half its capital in one sector. Which idea does this illustrate?
o: Ongoing manager review
Fund due diligence
Portfolio concentration review
Track record analysis
mocks.w: This is Portfolio concentration review. Reviewing the fund's concentration by company, sector and vintage reveals risks of overexposure.

mocks.p: A trust pools ₹100 crore from wealthy investors for private investments. Which idea does this illustrate?
o: Alternative Investment Fund
Category II AIF
Angel fund
Minimum investment
mocks.w: This is Alternative Investment Fund. An AIF is a privately pooled investment vehicle that raises money from investors for investing as per a defined policy, regulated by SEBI.

mocks.p: A fund where senior members have left raises concerns. Which idea does this illustrate?
o: Fund due diligence
Strategy fit
Concentration of investor base
Team stability
mocks.w: This is Team stability. Stability and depth of the investment team, incentives and succession are critical to the fund's success.

mocks.p: Investors vote to replace the manager though no wrongdoing is alleged. Which idea does this illustrate?
o: Governing law and disputes
No-fault removal
Default provisions
Investment management agreement
mocks.w: This is No-fault removal. A no-fault removal clause lets investors remove the manager by a supermajority vote without proving misconduct.

mocks.p: The manager gets 20% of profits above the hurdle. Which idea does this illustrate?
o: Carried interest
IRR and MOIC
DPI, RVPI and TVPI
Drawdown
mocks.w: This is Carried interest. Carried interest is the manager's share of fund profits, commonly 20%, earned after investors receive their capital and preferred return.

mocks.p: Which statement about “In-specie distribution” is correct?
o: In-specie means paying in foreign currency.
In-specie distribution gives investors the underlying securities instead of cash when the fund winds up or at exit.
The statement shows the manager's personal investments.
An IPO exit is not available to PE funds.
mocks.w: Correct: In-specie distribution gives investors the underlying securities instead of cash when the fund winds up or at exit.

mocks.p: A fund's performance is reported to an independent benchmarking provider. Which idea does this illustrate?
o: Concentration limit
Benchmarking and reporting
Distributor requirements
Direct plan
mocks.w: This is Benchmarking and reporting. AIFs must report performance to benchmarking agencies recognised by SEBI, supporting comparability and transparency.

mocks.p: A fund obtains a certificate before collecting commitments. Which idea does this illustrate?
o: Registration
Winding up
Leverage limits
Sponsor and manager commitment
mocks.w: This is Registration. An AIF must be registered with SEBI under one of the three categories before it raises funds.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Discounted cash flow” is correct?
o: The last round price is always right.
Comparable multiples need no peer companies.
DCF values an asset as the present value of expected future cash flows.
DCF uses only the last transaction price.
mocks.w: Correct: DCF values an asset as the present value of expected future cash flows.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Cost basis” is correct?
o: The last round price is always right.
Valuing at cost is acceptable only for a short period after investment, until better evidence is available.
Valuation has no link to fees.
Cost is the right basis for old investments.
mocks.w: Correct: Valuing at cost is acceptable only for a short period after investment, until better evidence is available.

mocks.p: Which statement about “Reference checks” is correct?
o: A single large investor makes a fund safer.
